A guest or news from far is said to be coming. Crows are also linked with the ancestors, and food is offered to them during the shraddha rites.
In many parts of India it is read as a sign to wait or to delay for a moment before going on; many people pause, or let someone else cross first.
Popularly said to mean trouble near, though most people see it as a sign that the dog has noticed something.
The owl is the vehicle of Lakshmi, and in some regions it is a good sign; in others its hooting at night near the home is considered a bad sign. Views are mixed.
Seeing a cow, especially on leaving the house, is considered auspicious in most of India.
Linked with Krishna and Kartikeya, and considered a good sign.
Seen as a good sign for a journey in some regions.
Sparrow building a nest in the house
Considered a sign of good luck and a happy home.
There is an old system (Gauli Shastra) that gives a different reading for each part of the body that a lizard falls on; it is a folk tradition, and many people simply wash and move on.
A bees' nest in or near a house is read in many places as a sign of good fortune, though people are advised to take care.
Seen as a sign of Ganesha and good fortune; meeting an elephant on the way is considered favourable.
In some regions, a snake crossing your path is a sign to turn back; in others it is a sign of good luck from the ancestors. Customs differ.
Tradition says that the right eye twitching is a good sign for men and the left eye for women, and the opposite for the other eye, but there are many versions.
In India, an itch on the right palm is said to mean money is coming, and on the left that money will go out; in some places it is the reverse.
A single sneeze when starting something is said to be a reason for a short pause; two sneezes are said to be a good sign.
Popularly said to mean that someone is remembering you.
In some places, the right ear ringing is said to mean that someone speaks well of you, and the left that someone speaks ill.
Said in some places to mean a journey coming.
Said in some places to mean food or a feast coming.
Yawning at the start of work
A reason to take a deep breath and begin again, as some elders say.
In a new home the milk boiling over is a favoured sign of overflowing prosperity, which is why it is done at griha pravesh.
A full pot of water, usually with a coconut and mango leaves, is a sign of abundance and is placed at the door for ceremonies; an empty pot seen at the start of a journey is read as a poor sign.
A spoonful of curd and sugar (dahi-cheeni) before an exam, an interview or a journey is a good-luck custom in many families.
In popular belief, a sign of a worry; the same belief is found in many countries, and most families simply clear it carefully.
Said to be a sign of a quarrel; the usual advice is to throw a pinch over the shoulder.
Said to be a reminder to look after the household; the lamp is lit again with a short prayer.
Cutting nails or hair at night
Elders in many families advise against it, usually with the practical reason of poor light.
Seeing a lit lamp at dusk
A sign of an auspicious evening and the blessing of Lakshmi.
Many families say to step out with the right foot first for a good start.
Seeing a full pot or a cow on leaving
Considered a good sign for a journey.
Being called back as you leave
In some families, it is a reason to sit down for a moment before setting out again.
If something goes wrong at the start of a journey, many people sit, drink water and begin again with a short prayer.
Taking sweets or curd before a journey
An old custom to wish a good journey and a good return.
Many people avoid beginning on days considered inauspicious in the panchang; see the Rahu Kaal section of this site for the traditional timings.
